content: Wheat allergy is a type of food allergy that can also manifest as a respiratory or contact allergy, particularly in individuals with occupational exposure to wheat. This condition involves an immune response mediated by Immunoglobulin E (IgE) and mast cells. The allergic reaction is typically directed against seed storage proteins in wheat, although some individuals may react to proteins found in other seeds and plant tissues. Wheat allergy is a complex condition, as wheat contains multiple allergenic components, such as serine proteinase inhibitors, glutelins, and prolamins, each capable of eliciting different immune responses. The most severe reaction associated with wheat allergy is exerciseor aspirin-induced anaphylaxis, which is linked to omega-gliadin, a protein related to the one responsible for celiac disease. Common symptoms of wheat allergy include nausea, hives (urticaria), and atopic conditions. Wheat contains four major classes of seed storage proteins: albumins, globulins, prolamins, and glutelins. Within wheat, prolamins are referred to as gliadins, and glutelins are called glutenins. Together, gliadins and glutenins form the classic gluten proteins. While gluten is a known trigger for celiac disease, wheat allergy differs in its immune mechanisms and the range of allergens involved, which extend beyond the classic gluten proteins. Prolamin allergies, particularly those involving gliadins, are associated with severe reactions. A Japanese study found that glutenins are more frequently allergenic, but gliadins are linked to the most severe cases. Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA) is primarily mediated by omega-5 gliadin, encoded by the Gli-1B gene derived from the Aegilops speltoides B genome in wheat. Glutelin allergies, specifically those involving low-molecular-weight glutenin subunits, are also significant contributors to wheat allergy. Albumin and globulin allergies are less well-characterized, but early studies identified many allergens within the albumin class. Recent European research has highlighted increased allergies to amylase/trypsin inhibitors (serpins) and lipid transfer proteins (LTPs), with less reactivity to the globulin fraction. These allergies vary among populations, suggesting a genetic component to the immune response. Respiratory allergies to wheat pollen and grass proteins are occupational hazards for food service workers. Studies have identified approximately 40 wheat allergens, some of which cross-react with rye proteins and grass pollens. Baker’s allergy, a form of occupational asthma, extends across a wide range of cereal grasses, with the strongest similarities observed between wheat and rye. Cross-reactivity between seed proteins and pollen proteins is common, particularly between rye pollen and wheat gluten. Hydrolyzed wheat proteins, created through enzymatic hydrolysis, can expose previously hidden antigenic sites, potentially creating new allergens. These hydrolyzed proteins are used as additives in foods and cosmetics and can cause immediate contact urticaria in sensitive individuals. Wheat allergy symptoms overlap with those of other food and respiratory allergies but are distinguished by the frequent occurrence of exercise/aspirin-induced anaphylaxis and urticaria. Common symptoms include eczema (atopic dermatitis), hives, asthma, allergic rhinitis, angioedema, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting. Rare symptoms include anaphylactic shock, arthritis, bloating, chest pain, depression, diarrhea, dizziness, headaches, joint and muscle pain, palpitations, psoriasis, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), throat or tongue swelling, fatigue, and unexplained coughing. Repeated exposure can exacerbate symptoms. Exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA) is associated with wheat gliadins and potentially oat avenins. During exercise, omega-gliadins or high-molecular-weight glutenin subunits enter the bloodstream, triggering acute allergic or asthmatic reactions. Aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can exacerbate WDEIA by increasing gliadin levels in the bloodstream. Baker’s allergy involves omega-gliadin and thioredoxin hB components, as well as Aspergillus amylase, an additive in flour. Contact sensitivity, atopic dermatitis, eczema, and urticaria are often linked to hydrophobic prolamin components, such as omega-gliadin. Studies suggest that avoiding wheat in the first year of life may prevent these conditions in sensitive individuals. Aspirin and other additives, such as tartrazine and MSG, may act as sensitizing factors. Wheat allergy has been associated with autoimmune rheumatoid arthritis (ARA) and gluten-sensitive enteropathy (GSE). In some cases, removing allergenic foods from the diet has improved ARA symptoms. Cross-reactive anti-beef-collagen antibodies may also contribute to rheumatoid arthritis in some individuals. Neurological conditions, such as migraines, have been linked to wheat allergy. Studies from the 1970s reported that eliminating wheat and other common allergens significantly reduced migraine frequency and hypertension. Autism has also been associated with wheat allergy, although evidence is limited and inconclusive. Acute psychosis has been linked to IgE antibodies against wheat and rye. Diagnosing wheat allergy can be challenging, as omega-5 gliadin, the most potent allergen, requires specific extraction and partial digestion to detect. Some allergy tests may fail to identify all wheat allergens, leading to cryptic allergies. Treatment involves avoiding wheat and related allergens. Unlike gluten exclusion for celiac disease, individuals with wheat allergy may tolerate barley and rye but are likely allergic to other wheat varieties, such as spelt and Kamut. Wheat is a hidden ingredient in many foods, including bread crumbs, maltodextrin, and modified starches, necessitating careful label reading. Alternative cereals, such as gluten-free oats, millet, buckwheat, quinoa, and rice flour, can be used as substitutes. However, spelt and Kamut are unsuitable for those with wheat allergy or celiac disease. Many individuals with wheat allergy are also allergic to soy, milk, and other food ingredients, requiring additional dietary adjustments.
